items.title: Advancing brain organoids from disease phenotypes to mechanisms and translation across developmental, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases
items.author: Jürgen A. Knoblich, Guo-li Ming, Sally Temple
items.content: <article>This review examines how human brain organoids are advancing studies of neurodevelopmental disorders, nervous system infections, and neurodegenerative diseases. It highlights emerging principles of cellular and temporal vulnerability, multicellular interactions, and disease progression and considers how improved reproducibility, benchmarking, and validation increase their value for therapeutic development and clinical translation.</article>

items.title: Neural organoid models of human brain evolution
items.author: Cicely F. Day, Alex A. Pollen, Madeline A. Lancaster
items.content: <article>Day et al. review how neural organoids enable experimental investigation of human brain evolution. They examine insights across biological scales, from genetic changes to cellular diversity and timing, and discuss the opportunities and limitations of these models for connecting evolutionary changes in DNA to brain development and function.</article>

items.title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development
items.author: Rahel Kastli, Rebecca E. Andersen, Christopher A. Walsh, Paola Arlotta
items.content: <article>Human brain development is largely inaccessible to mechanistic investigation, and evolutionarily divergent programs cannot be fully modeled in other species. Here, Kastli et al. review brain organoids as powerful experimental systems to unravel the mechanisms of human neurodevelopment and its neurodivergences.</article>

items.title: Toward functional oversight of neural organoid research: A report from the 2025 Asilomar Conference
items.author: Brie Linkenhoker
items.content: <article>In November 2025, an international multistakeholder group convened at Asilomar, California, to address oversight of rapidly advancing neural organoid and assembloid research. This process report documents the convening’s design, outcomes, and lessons, and it asks what it will take to turn this momentum into ongoing monitoring and practical guidelines that ensure responsible research without constraining scientific progress.</article>

items.title: Cognitive evaluation of brain organoids and assembloids
items.author: Lucia Melloni, Stanislas Dehaene
items.content: <article>The computational abilities of brain organoids and assembloids remain largely unexplored. We propose a hierarchy of assays grounded in cognitive neuroscience and probing representations, memory, and predictive processing, thus enabling causal tests of how architecture and maturation shape emerging computations while providing empirical constraints on debates about organoid consciousness.</article>

items.title: Unbundling the ethical and social issues in human neural organoid research
items.author: Henry T. Greely, Nita Farahany
items.content: <article>As human neural organoid research advances, some key concepts in its ethical analysis need to be unbundled to keep pace with scientific developments. These include interests involved in informed consent, distinct dimensions of consciousness and their implications for welfare, approaches to engaging public concerns, and governance and oversight of both organoids themselves and their uses.</article>

items.title: Human stem cell neuroscience
items.author: Sergiu P. Pașca
items.content: <article>In neuroscience, the most relevant human biology has often been the least accessible. Stem-cell-based models, such as organoids and assembloids, are opening ways to generate, assemble, probe, and perturb neural cells and circuits, helping define “stem cell neuroscience.” In this issue of Neuron, this and other reviews and commentaries discuss the current state of this emerging field.</article>
